text: What is the difference between an array and a linked list?
expected: Array: contiguous memory, O(1) index access, costly insert/delete in the middle. Linked list: nodes with pointers, O(n) access, O(1) insert/delete at a known node, grows dynamically, extra memory for pointers.

text: What is a stack, and where is it used?
expected: Last in, first out; push and pop in O(1); function call stack, undo, expression evaluation, bracket matching, depth-first search.

text: How is a queue different from a stack? Give one real use of a queue.
expected: First in, first out vs last in, first out; enqueue and dequeue; breadth-first search, CPU or printer scheduling, buffering requests.

text: What is a hash table, and what is a collision?
expected: Maps keys to bucket indexes with a hash function; average O(1) lookup; a collision is two keys mapping to the same bucket; handled by chaining or open addressing.

text: What is a binary search tree, and what property does it keep?
expected: Left subtree keys are smaller and right subtree keys are larger than the node; in-order traversal gives sorted order; search and insert take O(height).

text: What is the difference between breadth-first search and depth-first search?
expected: BFS explores level by level using a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS goes deep using a stack or recursion; both are O(V + E).

text: Why can a hash table's lookup slow down from O(1) to O(n), and how do you prevent it?
expected: Many collisions from a poor hash function or a high load factor; use a good hash function, resize and rehash around load factor 0.75, or use balanced trees in buckets.

text: Why does an unbalanced binary search tree become slow, and how do AVL or red-black trees fix it?
expected: Inserting sorted data makes it a linked list with O(n) height; self-balancing trees use rotations to keep the height O(log n).

text: Compare quicksort and merge sort. When would you choose each?
expected: Quicksort: average O(n log n), worst O(n^2), in place, cache friendly. Merge sort: always O(n log n), stable, needs O(n) extra space, good for linked lists and external sorting.

text: Why is a heap used for a priority queue instead of a sorted array?
expected: Heap insert and remove-min are O(log n) versus O(n) insertion in a sorted array; peek is O(1); a heap can be built in O(n).

text: How does a dynamic array, like a Python list or Java ArrayList, grow? Why is appending still O(1) on average?
expected: When full it allocates a bigger array (often double) and copies; the occasional O(n) copy is spread over many appends, so amortised cost is O(1).

text: When would you store a graph as an adjacency list rather than an adjacency matrix?
expected: Adjacency list for sparse graphs: O(V + E) space and fast neighbour iteration; matrix for dense graphs or O(1) edge lookups, at O(V^2) space.

text: How would you check whether the brackets in an expression like {[()]} are balanced?
expected: Scan left to right; push opening brackets; on a closing bracket pop and check it matches; the stack must be empty at the end; O(n).

text: How would you detect whether a linked list has a cycle?
expected: Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet if there is a cycle, O(n) time and O(1) space; or store visited nodes in a hash set, O(n) space.

text: In a metro map where every hop between stations takes the same time, how would you find the shortest route between two stations?
expected: Model stations as a graph with an adjacency list; run BFS from the source with a queue, keep parent pointers to rebuild the path; O(V + E); use Dijkstra if hops have different times.

text: How would you find the first non-repeating character in a string efficiently?
expected: Count each character with a hash map or a 26-slot array, then scan the string again for the first character with count 1; O(n) time.
